transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-30
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood SE), Greg Huang (Redwood SE), Olivia Chen (CardioHealth Head of Security), Dr. Marcus Lee (CardioHealth CTO), Elena Rossi (CardioHealth Compliance)

Summary (auto-gen, may be rough):
CardioHealth requests confirmation on data residency and region pinning options for US/EU; clarifications on cross-border processing, sub-processors, KMS/BYOK support, audit logs retention and RBAC/SSO integration. Redwood explains hosted vs dedicated vs private options and routing/fallback behavior. Action items and docs to be shared.

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir: All right good afternoon everyone, thanks for joining. This is Samir from Redwood, i'm joined by lena and greg. How are you all doing?
[00:10] Olivia: Hi Samir, hi lena, thanks. Olivia here. Quick note we're on a slightly delayed schedule so we might have to hop off at the 45 minute mark.
[00:17] Dr. Lee: Marcus here, thanks for doing this. We're mainly focused on residency and legal boundaries, so hoping to get specifics.
[00:25] Lena: Great totally fine, we'll keep it tight. Just to set context, we'll walk through our residency options, region pinning config, sub-processor disclosures, and encryption/KMS options, and then leave time for Qs.
[00:35] Samir: Quick intro - CardioHealth use case: clinical decision support and patient summarization, high-sensitivity PHI in some flows, correct?
[00:42] Elena: Yes, PHI plus some PII. We need EU patient data to remain in EU for storage and processing, and US for US. Cross-border processing is permitted only under specific circumstances and with contractual controls.
[00:55] Lena: Understood. Our platform supports three deployment modes: hosted, dedicated, and private. Hosted is our multi-tenant API but we offer region pinning inside hosted where requests from EU can be routed to EU-only capacity; Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools in a region; Private is VPC or on-prem for full isolation.
[01:20] Olivia: When you say "region pinning" how deterministic is routing? If EU is pinned, do requests ever egress to US for failover?
[01:30] Greg: Good question. By default we route by policy: you can pin by customer, by route, or by model. If you pin to eu-west-1 the primary serving plane and model variants are in EU. We do have fallback policies — you can opt into strict residency which disables cross-region fallback, or allow fallback for availability.
[01:50] Dr. Lee: Fallback disabled is what we want for EU patient data. We need guaranteed no processing outside EU. Also are sub-processors (cloud providers) located where you say?
[02:05] Lena: For strict residency we recommend Dedicated or Private. Hosted with strict pinning can meet many requirements but we still use cloud infra sub-processors — we publish a sub-processor list and their regions. For Dedicated the GPU fleet is dedicated and we can limit to specific cloud regions; Private gives you the most control — on-prem or VPC with customer-managed network.
[02:27] Olivia: Can you share the sub-processor roster and whether any analytics or logs are processed outside the region?
[02:35] Samir: Yes we'll send the current sub-processor list. Regarding logs: audit logs for admin control plane are retained in the control plane region; we offer options to mirror logs into customer S3 in their region, and embedded request logs can be configured to stay in-region. There's an operational control plane that may exist in a separate region for management traffic unless you're on Private where the control plane can be customer-managed.
[02:58] Elena: So for compliance we'd need assurance that the control plane telemetry doesn't include PHI and that any control plane backups are EU-resident.
[03:07] Greg: Correct; control plane telemetry excludes payloads by default. We store operational metadata and traces; payload-level logs are off by default and only enabled with explicit consent. For enterprise customers we can arrange retention and region policies — we'll document that.
[03:25] Dr. Lee: Encryption - do you support customer-managed keys (BYOK) and HSM-backed KMS? Where are keys stored?
[03:34] Lena: We support both vendor-managed and customer-managed keys. For Hosted we can integrate with customer KMS using envelope encryption; keys can remain in customer-managed KMS (e.g., AWS KMS in eu-west-1) and we store only wrapped keys. For Dedicated and Private you can bring keys into your VPC/HSM. We also have HSM integrations for higher assurance.
[03:56] Olivia: Is there an option for in-line encryption so payloads are never decrypted outside the customer's boundary?
[04:03] Samir: We have a design called “client-side encryption” — you encrypt sensitive fields before sending and embed decryption hooks in a private deployment. For hosted inference normal model execution requires decryption inside the serving runtime; for highest assurance we recommend Private with customer KMS where keys never leave your control. We'll send architecture notes.
[04:24] Elena: GDPR question: cross-border transfer legal mechanisms — do you provide SCCs or rely on customer contract addenda?
[04:32] Samir: We can provide standard SCCs in our DPA and we also support EU Data Processing Addendum that includes SCCs language. We'll attach the DPA and SCC references.
[04:43] Dr. Lee: Audit logs - retention and tamper evidence? We need immutable logs with retention 7 years for our audit.
[04:52] Greg: We support write-once storage for audit logs if required; logs can be exported to customer-controlled S3 with object lock/immutability for retention windows. We also sign logs with HSM-backed keys for tamper evidence. We'll include a diagram of the log pipeline.
[05:12] Olivia: Another point — sub-processors, do you rely on third-party model vendors or open checkpoints that may ping home?
[05:21] Lena: We curate open models and run them inside our runtime; we don't phone home model artifacts. Model updates are pulled from validated registries; we can sign and attest model binaries. Third-party telemetry won't be sent without consent.
[05:34] Elena: For SSO and RBAC — we use SAML and SCIM provisioning. How granular is role mapping for audit separation?
[05:43] Samir: We support SSO via SAML/OIDC and provisioning with SCIM. RBAC is role-based with resource scoping (per-organization, per-project, per-model). You can map SSO groups to roles and restrict who can view raw request payloads. All of that will be in the tenant-level policy UI and API.
[06:03] Dr. Lee: About region pinning config — what does the config look like? Is it per-route, per-API key?
[06:10] Greg: It's flexible — you can pin at account level, API key level, or route level. Example: set header 'X-Region-Pin: eu' or configure route policy in the console that pins chat/* to eu-west-1. We'll forward a sample policy file.
[06:25] Olivia: Are there performance implications of strict region pinning or disallowing fallback?
[06:30] Lena: Slightly, because strict pinning reduces our ability to route to lower-latency or lower-cost pools outside the region for burst. But for most steady workloads the impact is minimal. We'll share percentile latency comparisons for EU-only fleets vs cross-region fallback.
[06:47] Elena: Any impact on cost?
[06:50] Samir: Dedicated EU-only capacity can be priced slightly higher because of reserved GPUs, but we can model it for your traffic. Redwood Optimize can recommend batching and quantization profiles to keep costs predictable.
[07:02] Olivia: On the sub-processor list, what about AZ-level resilience inside EU only, not multi-region across borders.
[07:11] Greg: We can design for multi-AZ within a single region. For EU we typically run across two AZs in eu-west-1. Cross-region is optional and only used when allowed by policy.
[07:22] Dr. Lee: Incident response and breach notification timelines?
[07:26] Lena: Our standard SLA includes 72-hour notification for confirmed breaches plus periodic incident reports. For enterprise customers we can contract narrower timelines and detailed runbooks.
[07:38] Elena: Can you supply SOC 2 scope showing which systems are in or out of scope, especially around control plane and telemetry?
[07:45] Samir: Yes we'll attach our SOC 2 report and a scope summary that indicates data plane vs control plane boundaries.
[07:53] Olivia: Encryption-in-transit, at-rest — standard TLS and AES-256?
[07:59] Greg: Yes TLS 1.2+ in transit, AES-256 for at-rest, and we support customer-managed keys for envelope encryption.
[08:08] Dr. Lee: A more nuanced ask: Some of our countries require that derivative data (like embeddings or summaries) are also kept in-region. Is that supported?
[08:18] Lena: Yes you can configure retention policies per artifact type (raw payloads, embeddings, logs). Embeddings and derived outputs can be persisted in the same region and subject to the same pinning rules.
[08:30] Olivia: Operational question — who has access to production logs inside Redwood team? Need to know human access controls and sessions.
[08:38] Samir: We enforce least privilege, with RBAC and just-in-time access for engineers via our internal access system; all human access is logged and requires approvals for sensitive operations. We'll provide an access matrix and recent audit examples.
[08:54] Elena: For DPA clauses and audit rights, we might request onsite audits or evidence. What's Redwood's stance?
[09:00] Samir: We support remote audits and can arrange on-prem or detailed evidence packages for enterprise customers. Onsite audits are possible with a statement of work.
[09:09] Dr. Lee: How often do you publish sub-processor updates and how are customers notified?
[09:15] Lena: We publish on our compliance portal and send notices 30 days prior to onboarding new sub-processors; emergency patching exceptions have a shorter notice and are flagged in the portal.
[09:26] Olivia: Can you confirm whether third-party monitoring or APM providers ingest any request metadata?
[09:33] Greg: Traces include timing metadata but exclude payloads unless specifically configured. APM providers used for runtime health receive only anonymized metrics by default.
[09:42] Elena: We need to see example contractual language for region pinning and a DPA amendment we can insert into our master services agreement.
[09:50] Samir: We'll draft a sample clause for region-specific processing and an exhibit for the DPA.
[09:56] Olivia: Regarding backups — where are backups stored and how long retained?
[10:02] Lena: Backups for model artifacts and configuration can be stored regionally; for hosted customers we rotate backups and can set TTL. For enterprise you can request in-region backup retention with OLA for deletion and export.
[10:15] Dr. Lee: For legal: if we need to rely on SCCs, will Redwood sign DPAs referencing standard SCCs or is custom language needed?
[10:24] Samir: We provide standard SCCs in our DPA; for customized clauses we'll work with legal and have examples.
[10:32] Olivia: Ok this is helpful. Could you also include a sample traffic routing policy and an example request header to force EU processing?
[10:40] Greg: Yes sample header and policy file will be included in the follow-up.
[10:46] Elena: Anything else we should know about sub-processors in China or other restricted jurisdictions?
[10:52] Lena: We don't run production EU or US customer workloads on China-based sub-processors unless explicitly requested and contracted; any such arrangement would be elevated and documented.
[11:03] Dr. Lee: One more - SLA around deletion requests: when we call delete for a dataset, what is the timeline across caches, backups, and logs?
[11:11] Greg: Standard deletion for data plane objects is within 30 days; for backups and immutable logs it depends on retention and legal holds. For urgent deletions we provide an expedited path and confirmation of deletion across backups where possible — we'll outline procedures.
[11:27] Olivia: Are there any known gaps or product limitations with region pinning today we should be aware of?
[11:33] Lena: A couple: hosted strict pinning is available but edge caching and some third-party integrations might still touch metadata outside region — we document those exceptions. Dedicated and Private remove most of those limitations. We'll be transparent in the doc.
[11:49] Samir: To recap quickly: we'll send SOC2/ISO docs, sub-processor list, DPA + SCC sample, region pinning sample policy, architecture diagrams for hosted vs dedicated vs private, KMS/BYOK notes, log pipeline and export options, and proposed next steps for a private deployment deep dive.
[12:09] Olivia: Great, thanks. Any final compliance notes?
[12:12] Elena: We'd like to include the legal team on the next thread.
[12:16] Samir: Perfect, we'll cc legal. Thanks everyone.
[12:20] Dr. Lee: Thanks all.

(End of captured transcript - timestamps after 12:20 mark represent first ~12 minutes of the call; caller indicated 45 minute duration, remainder of call was Q&A and scheduling, summary and next steps captured above.)
